chapters.title: Book 1
paragraphs: 1. From my grandfather Verus I learned good character and control of my temper.
2. From my father's reputation and my memory of him: modesty and a manly character.

3. From my mother: reverence for the gods and generosity; holding back not only from doing wrong, but even from thinking of it; and also a simple way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich.

4. From my great-grandfather: not to have been sent to the public schools open to everyone, but to have had good teachers at home, and to know that on an education like this one should spend generously.

5. From my tutor: not to be a supporter of either the Green or the Blue faction at the races in the Circus, nor a fan of either the Parmularius or the Scutarius, the light-shield and heavy-shield fighters, at the gladiator fights. From him, too, I learned to endure hard work and to want little; to work with my own hands; not to meddle in other people's affairs; and not to be quick to listen to slander.

6. From Diognetus: not to busy myself with trivial things; not to believe what miracle-workers and conjurers say about spells and driving out spirits and things of that kind; not to breed quails for fighting, or get carried away by such pastimes; and to put up with people speaking their minds freely. It was through him, too, that I became at home with philosophy, and heard the lectures first of Bacchius, then of Tandasis and Marcianus; that I wrote dialogues when I was young; and that I wanted a plank bed and an animal skin to sleep on, and whatever else of that kind belongs to the Greek philosophical training.

7. From Rusticus I got the impression that my character needed correcting and training. From him I learned not to be drawn into ambition to shine as a sophist, a showman of clever speeches, nor into writing about abstract theories, nor into delivering little moral sermons, nor into parading myself as a man of strict self-discipline, or as someone who does good deeds for show. I learned from him to keep away from rhetoric, poetry and fancy writing; not to walk around the house in my outdoor clothes, or do other things of that kind; to write my letters plainly, like the letter Rusticus wrote to my mother from Sinuessa; to be easily calmed and reconciled with those who have offended me in words or done me wrong, as soon as they show they are willing to be reconciled; to read carefully, and not be satisfied with a rough grasp of a book; and not to be quick to agree with people who talk too much. And I owe it to him that I came to know the discourses of Epictetus, which he shared with me from his own collection.

8. From Apollonius I learned freedom of will and a firm purpose that does not waver; never, even for a moment, to look to anything but reason; to be always the same—in sharp pain, at the loss of a child, in long illness; to see clearly, in a living example, that the same man can be both very determined and easygoing, and not irritable when teaching; to have had before my eyes a man who plainly regarded his experience and his skill in explaining philosophical principles as the least of his merits; and from him I learned how to accept what are counted as favors from friends, without either being humbled by them or letting them pass unacknowledged.

9. From Sextus: kindliness; the example of a household governed by a father's care; the idea of living in keeping with nature, that is, as nature made a human being to live; dignity without pretense; careful attention to the interests of friends; patience with ignorant people, and with those who form opinions without thinking. He could adapt himself easily to everyone, so that his company was more pleasant than any flattery, and yet those who spent time with him held him in the highest respect. He had the ability to discover the principles we need for living, and to set them in order intelligently and methodically. He never showed anger or any other passion; he was entirely free from passion—from disturbing emotion—and yet full of affection. He could express approval without fuss, and he had great learning without showing it off.

10. From Alexander the grammarian: not to be a fault-finder, and not to scold people who use an uncouth, ungrammatical or odd-sounding expression, but tactfully to bring in the very expression that should have been used—in the course of an answer, or while agreeing with them, or while joining them in looking into the matter itself rather than the word, or by some other fitting hint.

11. From Fronto I learned to notice what envy, deceit and hypocrisy are like in a tyrant; and that, on the whole, those among us who are called Patricians are rather lacking in natural, fatherly affection.

12. From Alexander the Platonist: not to say often to anyone, or write in a letter, without real need, that I have no time; and not to keep excusing myself from the duties we owe to the people we live with by pleading urgent business.

13. From Catulus: not to shrug it off when a friend finds fault, even if he finds fault without reason, but to try to bring him back to his usual frame of mind; to be ready to speak well of teachers, as is reported of Domitius and Athenodotus; and to love my children truly.

14. From my brother Severus: to love my family, to love truth, and to love justice. Through him I came to know of Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion and Brutus. From him I received the idea of a state with the same law for everyone, governed on the basis of equal rights and equal freedom of speech, and the idea of a monarchy that respects above all the freedom of those it governs. From him I also learned to value philosophy steadily and consistently; to be ready to do good and quick to give; to stay hopeful; and to trust that my friends love me. I saw in him that he never hid his opinion of those he condemned, and that his friends never had to guess what he wanted or did not want; it was plain.

15. From Maximus I learned self-control, and not to be swayed by anything; to be cheerful in all circumstances, illness included; a character with the right blend of gentleness and dignity; and to do the work in front of me without complaining. I saw that everyone believed he meant what he said, and that whatever he did, he did with no bad intent. He was never astonished or startled, never in a hurry, never put things off; he was never at a loss or downcast; he never laughed to hide his irritation, nor, on the other hand, was he ever quick-tempered or suspicious. He was in the habit of doing kindnesses, ready to forgive, and free from all falsehood. He gave the impression of a man who could not be turned from what was right, not of a man who had had to be set right. I noticed, too, that no one could ever think Maximus looked down on him, or ever venture to think himself the better man. He also had the gift of being pleasantly humorous.

16. In my father I saw gentleness, and unshakable firmness in decisions he had reached after careful thought; no vanity about the things people call honors; a love of work, and persistence; readiness to listen to anyone who had something to propose for the common good; unwavering firmness in giving everyone what he deserved; and the knowledge, gained from experience, of when to act vigorously and when to ease off. I saw that he had overcome all passion for boys; that he thought of himself as no more than any other citizen; that he freed his friends from any obligation to dine with him or to travel with him when he went away; and that those who had been kept from going with him by some urgent business always found him unchanged toward them. I saw how carefully he looked into every matter he had to decide, and how persistently, and that he never cut his inquiry short because he was satisfied with first impressions. I saw that it was his way to keep his friends, neither tiring of them quickly nor being extravagant in his affection; to be content in every situation, and cheerful; to see far ahead, and to take care of the smallest matters without fuss; to put an immediate stop to public applause and all flattery; to keep constant watch over what the government of the empire needed; to manage its spending carefully; and to put up patiently with the criticism he got for doing so. He was not superstitious about the gods, and he did not try to win people over with gifts, or by pleasing them, or by flattering the crowd; he showed moderation and steadiness in everything, never anything petty or base in thought or action, and no craving for novelty. The things that make life comfortable, which fortune supplied him in plenty, he used without arrogance and without apology: when he had them, he enjoyed them without pretense, and when he did not have them, he did not miss them. No one could ever have called him a sophist, or a pert, flippant slave raised in the house, or a pedant; everyone recognized him as a mature and complete man, above flattery, able to manage both his own affairs and other people's. Besides this, he honored those who were true philosophers; he did not scorn those who only pretended to be philosophers, but he was not easily led by them either. He was easy to talk to, and he made himself pleasant without any tiresome affectation. He took reasonable care of his health—not as someone clinging to life, nor out of concern for his looks, nor yet carelessly—so that, thanks to his own attention, he very seldom needed a doctor's skill, or medicines, or ointments. He was very ready, and without envy, to give way to people who had some special ability, such as eloquence, or knowledge of the law or of morals, or of anything else; and he helped them, so that each might have the reputation he deserved. He always acted according to the ancestral customs of his country, without making a show of doing so. Further, he did not like change and was not restless; he liked to stay in the same places and busy himself with the same things. After his attacks of headache he went straight back, fresh and vigorous, to his usual work. He had few secrets—very few, and only rarely—and those only about public matters. He was sensible and sparing in putting on public shows, in constructing public buildings, in his gifts to the people and in things of that kind, for he was a man who looked at what needed to be done, not at the reputation to be gained from doing it. He did not bathe at odd hours; he was not fond of building houses; he was not particular about his food, or about the weave and color of his clothes, or about the good looks of his slaves. His clothes came from Lorium, his villa on the coast, and from Lanuvium generally. We know how he treated the toll-collector at Tusculum who asked his pardon; and all his behavior was like that. There was nothing harsh about him, nothing unforgiving or violent, nothing forced, nothing, as they say, carried to the point of sweating. He examined everything item by item, as if he had all the time in the world—calmly, in an orderly way, vigorously and consistently. What is recorded of Socrates could be said of him: he could do without the things that most people are too weak to do without, and he could enjoy the things that most people cannot enjoy without excess. To be strong enough both to hold out when one lacks such things and to stay sober when one has them is the mark of a man with a perfect and unconquerable soul, such as he showed during the illness of Maximus.

17. To the gods I owe it that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good companions, good relatives and friends—almost everything good. I owe it to the gods, too, that I was never rushed into offending any of the gods, though I had the kind of temperament that, given the chance, might have led me to do something of the sort; but by their favor things never came together in a way that put me to the test. I am grateful to the gods, too, that I was not brought up any longer with my grandfather's mistress; that I kept the freshness of my youth, and did not prove my manhood before the proper time, but even put it off; that I was placed under a ruler and father who could strip all pride from me and bring me to see that a man can live in a palace without needing bodyguards, or embroidered robes, or torches and statues and that kind of show—that such a man can bring himself very close to the way a private citizen lives, without being on that account any less noble in thought or any slacker in action when it comes to doing what must be done for the public good in the way that befits a ruler. I thank the gods that I had such a brother, whose character could rouse me to keep watch over myself, and who at the same time gladdened me with his respect and affection; that my children have been neither dull-witted nor deformed in body; that I did not get further in rhetoric, poetry and the other studies, which might perhaps have taken me over completely if I had seen myself making progress in them; that I was quick to give the people who brought me up the position of honor they seemed to want, instead of putting them off with the hope that I would do it later, on the grounds that they were still young; that I knew Apollonius, Rusticus and Maximus; that I received clear and frequent impressions of what it is to live in keeping with nature, and what kind of life that is—so that, as far as it depended on the gods and their gifts, help and inspiration, nothing stopped me from living in keeping with nature at once, though I still fall short of it through my own fault, and through not heeding the gods' reminders and, I might almost say, their direct instructions; I thank the gods, too, that my body has held out so long in the kind of life I lead; that I never touched either Benedicta or Theodotus, and that, after I did fall into passions of love, I was cured; that though I was often annoyed with Rusticus, I never did anything I had cause to regret; that, although it was my mother's fate to die young, she spent her last years with me; that whenever I wanted to help someone in need, or on any other occasion, I was never told that I did not have the means; and that I myself never fell into the same need, of having to accept anything from someone else; that I have such a wife—so obedient, so affectionate, so unpretentious; that I had plenty of good teachers for my children; that remedies have been shown to me in dreams, both for other ailments and against spitting blood and dizziness...; and that when I became drawn to philosophy I did not fall into the hands of any sophist, and did not waste my time on writers of histories, or on solving logical syllogisms, or on studying the phenomena of the sky. For all these things need the help of the gods and of fortune. Written among the Quadi, on the Granua.

chapters.title: Book 2
paragraphs: 1. Begin each morning by telling yourself: today I shall meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, and careless of others. They are like this because they do not know what is good and what is bad. But I have seen what the good is, and that it is noble; and what the bad is, and that it is shameful. And I have seen what the wrongdoer himself is: he is my kin—not only because we share the same blood or seed, but because we share the same intelligence and the same portion of the divine. So none of them can harm me, since none of them can drag me into anything shameful. Nor can I be angry with my kinsman or hate him. For we were made to work together, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the upper and lower rows of teeth. To work against one another, then, is against nature; and to resent someone and turn away from him is to work against him.

2. Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh, a little breath, and the ruling faculty—the reasoning mind that governs the rest of me. Throw away your books; stop letting yourself be distracted; that is no longer allowed. Instead, as though you were already dying, think nothing of the flesh: it is blood and bones and a network, a woven tangle of nerves, veins and arteries. Look at the breath too, and see what it is: air, and never the same air, but every moment breathed out and drawn in again. The third part, then, is the ruling faculty. Consider this: you are an old man, so do not let this part be a slave any longer. Do not let it be jerked on strings like a puppet by impulses that set you against others. Do not let it be discontented any longer with what you have been given now, or shrink from what is to come.

3. Everything that comes from the gods is full of providence—the gods' care and foresight. Even what comes from fortune is not separate from nature; it is woven and bound together with the things that providence directs. Everything flows from providence. Necessity plays its part too, and so does what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part. Whatever the nature of the universe brings about, and whatever keeps that nature in being, is good for every part of nature. And the universe is kept in being by change: by the changes of the elements, and equally by the changes of the things made from the elements. Let these principles be enough for you; hold them always as settled judgments. But throw away your thirst for books, so that you do not die grumbling, but cheerfully, sincerely, and grateful to the gods from your heart.

4. Remember how long you have been putting all this off, and how many times the gods have given you an opportunity that you have not used. It is time now, at last, to understand what universe you are a part of, and who governs that universe—the one from whom your own existence flows. Understand, too, that a limit has been set to your time. If you do not use it to clear the clouds from your mind, it will pass, and you will pass, and it will never come back.

5. Every moment, set your mind firmly, as a Roman and a man, on doing the task in front of you with complete and unpretentious dignity, with warmth, freedom and justice. And set it on freeing yourself from every other thought. You will free yourself if you do each act of your life as if it were your last: without carelessness, without the passionate aversion that turns away from what reason commands, without pretense, without self-love, and without discontent with the share you have been given. You see how few things there are: whoever holds on to them is able to live a life that flows quietly, like the life of the gods. For the gods, on their part, will ask nothing more of someone who keeps to these things.

6. Go on, keep wronging yourself, my soul, keep wronging yourself! But you will no longer have the chance to honor yourself. Each person's life is enough; but yours is nearly over, and still you do not respect yourself, but make your happiness depend on the souls of others.

7. Do the things that happen to you from outside distract you? Then give yourself time to learn something new and good, and stop being spun around. But you must also guard against being carried off in the other direction. For some people wear themselves out with activity all their lives, yet have no goal toward which to direct every impulse and, in short, every thought; and they too are wasting their lives on trifles.
8. People are seldom made unhappy by failing to notice what goes on in someone else's mind; but those who do not pay attention to the movements of their own minds are bound to be unhappy.

9. Always keep this in mind: what the nature of the whole is, and what my own nature is; how the one is related to the other; and what kind of part mine is, and of what kind of whole. And remember that no one can stop you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part.

10. Theophrastus, comparing wrong acts as one would compare them by ordinary human standards, says, like a true philosopher, that wrongs done out of desire deserve more blame than wrongs done out of anger. For someone who is gripped by anger seems to turn away from reason with a kind of pain, and a shrinking inside that he is not aware of. But someone who does wrong out of desire, overcome by pleasure, seems in a way more self-indulgent and more womanish in his wrongdoing. So he was right, and spoke as a philosopher should, when he said that a wrong done with pleasure deserves more blame than one done with pain. In general, the angry person is more like someone who has first been wronged and is driven to anger by the pain of it; the other has set out to do wrong on his own impulse, carried into the act by desire.

11. Since you may leave life at any moment, let that thought govern everything you do and think. If there are gods, leaving the company of human beings is nothing to fear, for the gods would not involve you in anything bad. And if there are no gods, or if they do not care about human affairs, why should I want to live in a universe without gods, or without providence? But in fact they do exist, and they do care about human affairs, and they have put it entirely in a person's power not to fall into what is truly bad. As for everything else, if any of it were bad, they would have provided for that too, so that it would be entirely in a person's power not to fall into it. And how can something that does not make a person worse make that person's life worse? If such things were bad, the nature of the universe could not have let them slip past it—not from ignorance, and not from knowing about them but lacking the power to prevent or correct them. Nor could it have made so great a mistake, through lack of power or lack of skill, that good and bad things would fall without distinction on good people and bad. Yet death and life, honor and dishonor, pain and pleasure all happen equally to good people and bad, and they make us neither better nor worse. Therefore they are neither good nor bad.

12. How quickly everything vanishes: the bodies themselves vanish into the universe, and even the memory of them vanishes into time. Consider what all the things the senses perceive really are—especially those that lure us with the bait of pleasure, or frighten us with pain, or are made famous by empty reputation—how worthless, contemptible, dirty, perishable and dead they are. It is the work of our power of understanding to observe this. It should observe, too, who these people are whose opinions and voices make a reputation. And it should observe what death is: if a person looks at death by itself, and by the power of thought takes apart everything the imagination has attached to it, he will see that it is nothing but a process of nature; and anyone who is afraid of a process of nature is a child. Yet death is not only a process of nature; it also serves nature's purposes. And it should observe how a human being comes near to God, through what part of himself he does so, and in what condition that part is when he does.

13. Nothing is more wretched than a person who runs around in circles after everything, and pries into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and tries to guess what is going on in his neighbors' minds, without realizing that it is enough to attend to the divine spirit within him—the guiding mind that is his share of the divine—and to honor it sincerely. And honoring it means keeping it pure from passion, from thoughtlessness, and from discontent with what comes from gods and human beings. For what comes from the gods deserves reverence because of its excellence. What comes from human beings should be dear to us because we are kin; and sometimes, in a way, it even moves our pity, because people do not know good from bad—a blindness no less serious than the one that leaves us unable to tell white from black.

14. Even if you were going to live three thousand years, or ten thousand times that, still remember that no one loses any life except the one he is living now, and no one lives any life except the one he is losing. So the longest life and the shortest come to the same thing. For the present moment is the same for everyone, even though the time that has passed away is not the same for all; and so what is lost turns out to be a mere moment. No one can lose the past or the future: how could anyone take from a person what he does not have? So you must keep these two things in mind. First, that all things have had the same forms from eternity and come round again in a circle, and that it makes no difference whether a person watches the same things for a hundred years, or two hundred, or for endless time. Second, that the person who lives longest and the person who dies soonest lose exactly the same. For the present is the only thing anyone can be deprived of—if it is true that it is the only thing he has, and that no one can lose what he does not have.

15. Remember that everything is opinion—what we judge things to be. For what the Cynic Monimus said is plain; and plain too is how useful his saying is, if you take from it what it has to offer, as far as it is true.

16. The human soul does violence to itself, first of all, when it becomes, as far as it can, an abscess, a kind of tumor on the universe. For to resent anything that happens is to break away from nature, which holds within it, each in its part, the natures of all other things. Second, the soul does violence to itself when it turns away from another person, or even goes at him meaning to harm him, as the souls of angry people do. Third, when it is overcome by pleasure or by pain. Fourth, when it puts on an act, and does or says anything falsely or insincerely. Fifth, when it lets any act or impulse of its own go without an aim, and does anything thoughtlessly, without considering what it is doing. For even the smallest things ought to be done for a purpose; and the purpose of rational beings is to follow the reason and the law of the oldest city and commonwealth of all—the universe itself.

17. In human life, time is a point; the stuff we are made of is always flowing; our perception is dim; the whole body, as it is put together, is prone to rot; the soul is a whirl; fortune is hard to predict; and fame has no judgment. In a word, everything belonging to the body is a river, and everything belonging to the soul is a dream and a vapor; life is a war and a stay in a foreign land; and after fame comes oblivion. What, then, can guide a person through it? One thing, and only one: philosophy. And philosophy means keeping the divine spirit within a person safe from violence and harm, stronger than pains and pleasures; doing nothing without a purpose, and nothing falsely or hypocritically; not needing anyone else to do or not do anything; accepting everything that happens and everything that is given to him as coming from the same source he himself came from, wherever that source may be; and, finally, waiting for death with a cheerful mind, since death is nothing but the breaking up of the elements that every living being is made of. And if the elements themselves come to no harm in constantly changing into one another, why should anyone fear the change and breaking up of all of them? It is in keeping with nature, and nothing that is in keeping with nature is bad. Written at Carnuntum.

chapters.title: Book 3
paragraphs: 1. We ought to consider not only that our life is wasting away day by day, and that less of it is left, but something else as well. If a person lives longer, it is quite uncertain whether his understanding will still be equal to grasping things, and whether it will keep the power of contemplation that strives for knowledge of the divine and the human. For if he begins to slide into senility, he will not stop perspiring and taking nourishment, or having imagination and appetite, or anything else of that kind. But the power to make use of ourselves, to fulfil the full measure of our duty, to sort out clearly everything that appears to us, to consider whether it is now time for a person to leave life, and whatever else of that kind absolutely requires a trained reason—all this has already gone out. So we must hurry, not only because every day brings us nearer to death, but also because our grasp and understanding of things is the first thing to fail.

2. We ought to notice, too, that even the things that come about as side effects of what nature produces have something pleasing and attractive about them. For instance, when bread is baked, some parts split open at the surface. These cracks take a shape that goes against what the baker's art intended, yet in a way they are beautiful, and they have their own particular way of making us want to eat. Again, figs split open when they are fully ripe; and in ripe olives, the very fact that they are close to rotting gives the fruit a beauty of its own. The ears of grain bending down, the lion's brow, the foam that flows from the mouths of wild boars, and many other things are far from beautiful if you look at them one by one. Still, because they follow from things that nature forms, they help to adorn them and they please the mind. So if a person has a feeling for the things produced in the universe, and a deeper insight into them, there is hardly one of these side effects that will not seem to him arranged, in its own way, to give pleasure. He will look at the real gaping jaws of wild beasts with no less pleasure than at the ones painters and sculptors imitate. In an old woman or an old man he will be able to see a certain ripeness and grace; and he will be able to look at the attractive loveliness of the young with chaste eyes. Many such things will present themselves. They do not please everyone, but only the person who has become truly familiar with nature and her works.

3. Hippocrates cured many diseases, then fell sick himself and died. The Chaldaeans foretold the deaths of many people, and then fate caught them too. Alexander, Pompeius and Caius Caesar so often destroyed whole cities completely, and cut to pieces many tens of thousands of cavalry and infantry in battle; yet in the end they too left life. Heraclitus speculated so much about the universe ending in fire, and then he was filled with water inside and died smeared all over with mud. Lice destroyed Democritus; and other lice killed Socrates. What does all this mean? You have gone on board, you have made the voyage, you have come to shore: get out. If it is to another life, there is no lack of gods, not even there. But if it is to a state without sensation, you will no longer be held by pains and pleasures, and you will stop being a slave to the vessel, the body. The vessel is as much inferior as the part that serves it is superior: for the one is intelligence and the divine; the other is earth and decay.

4. Do not waste what is left of your life in thoughts about other people, when you are not relating those thoughts to something that serves the common good. For when you have such thoughts, you lose the chance to do something else. Thoughts like these: What is so-and-so doing, and why? What is he saying? What is he thinking about? What is he scheming? These, and everything else of the kind, make us wander away from watching over our own ruling faculty. So in the chain of our thoughts we ought to check everything that is aimless and useless, and most of all whatever is over-curious or malicious. A person should train himself to think only about things of this sort: if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking about right now?”, you could answer at once and with complete openness, “This” or “That.” Then it would be plain from your words that everything in you is simple and kind, as befits a being made for community; that you do not care at all for thoughts of pleasure or sensual enjoyment; and that you have no rivalry, envy or suspicion, or anything else you would blush to admit was in your mind. For someone like this, who no longer puts off taking his place among the best, is a kind of priest and servant of the gods. He also makes use of the divine spirit planted within him, which keeps him unstained by pleasure, unharmed by any pain, untouched by any insult, and unable to feel wronged. He is a fighter in the noblest of fights; no passion can overpower him; he is dyed deep with justice; and he welcomes with all his soul everything that happens and is given to him as his share. Only rarely, and only when it is really necessary and for the common good, does he imagine what someone else is saying or doing or thinking. For he makes only what belongs to himself the material of his activity. He keeps constantly in mind the share that has been allotted to him out of the whole sum of things. He makes his own acts noble, and he is convinced that his own portion is good. For the lot assigned to each person is carried along with him, and carries him along with it. He remembers, too, that every rational being is his kin, and that caring for all human beings is in keeping with human nature. Yet a person should hold on to the opinion not of everyone, but only of those who clearly live in keeping with nature. As for those who do not live that way, he always bears in mind what sort of people they are, at home and away from home, by night and by day; what they are; and with what sort of people they live their impure lives. So he places no value at all on praise from such people, since they are not even satisfied with themselves.

5. Do not work unwillingly, or without regard for the common good, or without proper thought, or while your attention is pulled in different directions. Do not dress up your thoughts in fancy language. Do not be a person of many words, or one who is busy with too many things. Further, let the divine spirit within you be the guardian of a living being who is manly and mature, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler. Let him be someone who has taken up his post like a person waiting for the signal that calls him out of life: ready to go, and needing neither an oath nor anyone's testimony. Be cheerful, too, and do not look for help from outside, or for the calm that other people give. A person must stand upright, then, not be held upright by others.

6. Suppose you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control and courage. Suppose, in a word, you find anything better than your own mind being content with itself: content in the things it lets you do according to right reason, and content with the condition assigned to you without your choosing. If, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with all your soul, and enjoy what you have found to be the best. But suppose nothing appears better than the divine spirit planted in you: the spirit that has brought all your impulses under its control, that carefully examines every impression, that, as Socrates said, has pulled itself away from the persuasions of the senses, that has submitted itself to the gods, and that cares for human beings. If you find everything else smaller and of less worth than this, give room to nothing else. For once you turn aside and lean toward something else, you will no longer be able, without being torn, to give first place to the good that properly belongs to you and is your own. It is not right for anything of a different kind—such as praise from the crowd, or power, or the enjoyment of pleasure—to compete with what is good for a rational being and a member of the community. All these things, even if they seem to fit in with the better things to a small degree, suddenly take the upper hand and carry us away. But you, I say, simply and freely choose what is better, and hold on to it. “But what is useful is better.” Very well: if it is useful to you as a rational being, keep to it. But if it is useful to you only as an animal, say so, and keep to your judgment without arrogance. Only make sure that you examine the question by a sound method.

7. Never value anything as good for you if it will force you to break your word, to lose your self-respect, to hate anyone, to suspect, to curse, to be a hypocrite, or to want anything that needs walls and curtains to hide it. For someone who has put his own intelligence and divine spirit, and the worship of its excellence, before everything else does not put on a tragic act, does not groan, and will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Most important of all, he will live without either chasing death or running from it. Whether his soul is to be held within his body for a longer time or a shorter one, he does not care at all. Even if he must leave at once, he will go as readily as if he were going to do anything else that can be done with decency and order. All through life he takes care of this one thing only: that his thoughts never turn away from anything that belongs to an intelligent being and a member of a civic community.

8. In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and purified you will find nothing festering, nothing foul, no sore that has skinned over. Nor is his life left unfinished when fate overtakes him, as one might say of an actor who leaves the stage before the play has reached its end and is complete. Besides, there is nothing in him slavish or pretentious; nothing too tightly bound to other things, nor yet cut off from them; nothing that deserves blame; nothing that looks for a hiding place.

9. Honor the faculty that forms opinions. It depends entirely on this faculty whether your ruling faculty will hold any opinion that is out of keeping with nature and with the makeup of a rational being. And this faculty promises freedom from hasty judgment, friendship toward human beings, and obedience to the gods.

10. Throw everything else away, then, and hold on to these few things only. And remember, too, that each person lives only this present moment, which is an indivisible point; all the rest of his life is either already past or uncertain. Short, then, is the time each person lives; small is the corner of the earth where he lives; and short, too, is even the longest fame after death. And even that fame is kept going only by a succession of poor human beings who will very soon die, and who do not know even themselves, much less someone who died long ago.

11. To the aids already mentioned, add this one more. Make for yourself a definition or description of whatever presents itself to you, so that you see clearly what kind of thing it is in its substance: stripped bare, whole and entire. Tell yourself its proper name, and the names of the things it has been put together from and into which it will break up again. For nothing so lifts up the mind as being able to examine, methodically and truthfully, every object that comes before you in life. It means always looking at things in such a way as to see at the same time what kind of universe this is; what use each thing serves in it; what value each thing has in relation to the whole, and what value in relation to a human being, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which all other cities are like households. It means seeing what each thing is, what it is made of, and how long it is in its nature to last—this thing that is now making an impression on me—and what virtue I need in dealing with it: gentleness, manly courage, truthfulness, faithfulness, simplicity, contentment and the rest. So on every occasion a person should say: This comes from God. This comes by the allotting and spinning of the thread of destiny, and by coincidence and chance of that kind. And this comes from someone of my own stock, my kinsman and partner, who does not know, however, what is in keeping with his nature. But I know. So I treat him with kindness and justice, as the natural law of fellowship requires. At the same time, in things that are indifferent—neither good nor bad in themselves—I try to work out the value of each.

12. If you do the work in front of you by following right reason seriously, energetically and calmly, not letting anything else distract you, but keeping your divine part pure, as if you had to give it back at once; if you hold to this, expecting nothing and fearing nothing, but content with acting now in keeping with nature, and with speaking heroic truth in every word and sound you utter, then you will live happily. And there is no one who can stop you.

13. Doctors always keep their instruments and knives at hand for cases that suddenly call for their skill. In the same way, keep your principles ready for understanding things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, with the bond that joins the divine and the human to each other in mind. For you will never do anything well in human affairs without relating it at the same time to the divine; nor the other way round.

14. Stop wandering aimlessly. You are not going to read your own memoirs, or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks, or the passages from books that you were saving for your old age. Hurry on, then, toward the end that lies before you. Throw away empty hopes, and come to your own rescue while you still can, if you care for yourself at all.

15. People do not know how many things are meant by the words “stealing,” “sowing,” “buying,” “keeping quiet,” and “seeing what ought to be done.” For this is not done with the eyes, but with another kind of sight.

16. Body, soul, intelligence. To the body belong sensations; to the soul, impulses; to the intelligence, principles. To receive the stamp of impressions from the way things appear belongs even to animals. To be jerked on the strings of desire belongs to wild beasts, to men who have made themselves into women, and to a Phalaris or a Nero. And to have intelligence as a guide to what seems fitting belongs also to people who do not believe in the gods, who betray their country, and who do their impure deeds once they have shut the doors. If, then, everything else is shared by all those I have mentioned, what remains that is special to the good person is this: to be pleased and content with what happens and with the thread that is spun for him; not to defile the divine spirit planted in his breast, or disturb it with a crowd of images, but to keep it at peace, following it obediently as a god, saying nothing contrary to the truth and doing nothing contrary to justice. And if everyone refuses to believe that he lives a simple, modest and contented life, he is not angry with any of them. Nor does he turn aside from the road that leads to the end of life, where a person ought to arrive pure, at peace, ready to leave, and perfectly reconciled to his lot without any compulsion.

chapters.title: Book 4
paragraphs: 1. The ruling part, when it is according to nature, is so disposed toward the events that happen that it always adapts itself easily to what is possible and is presented to it. For it requires no definite material, but it moves toward its purpose, under certain conditions, however; and it makes a material for itself out of what opposes it, as fire lays hold of what falls into it, by which a small light would have been put out; but when the fire is strong, it soon makes its own the matter heaped on it, and consumes it, and rises higher by means of this very material.
2. Let no act be done without a purpose, nor otherwise than according to the perfect principles of art.

3. Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, seashores, and mountains; and you too are in the habit of wanting such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in your power, whenever you choose, to retire into yourself. For nowhere does a man retire with more quiet or more freedom from trouble than into his own soul, particularly when he has within him such thoughts that by looking into them he is at once in perfect calm; and I affirm that calm is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind. Constantly, then, give yourself this retreat, and renew yourself; and let your principles be brief and fundamental, which, as soon as you turn to them, will be enough to cleanse the soul completely, and to send you back free from all discontent with the things you return to. For what are you discontented with? With the badness of men? Recall to your mind this conclusion, that rational beings exist for one another, and that to endure is a part of justice, and that men do wrong involuntarily; and consider how many already, after mutual enmity, suspicion, hatred, and fighting, have been stretched out dead, reduced to ashes; and be quiet at last.—But perhaps you are discontented with what is assigned to you out of the universe.—Recall to your mind this alternative: either there is providence or there are atoms, a chance concurrence of things; or remember the arguments by which it has been proved that the world is a kind of political community; and be quiet at last.—But perhaps bodily things will still fasten on you.—Consider, then, further that the mind does not mingle with the breath, whether it moves gently or violently, once it has drawn itself apart and discovered its own power; and think also of all that you have heard and assented to about pain and pleasure; and be quiet at last.—But perhaps the desire for the thing called fame will torment you.—See how soon everything is forgotten, and look at the chaos of infinite time on each side of the present, and the emptiness of applause, and the changeableness and lack of judgment in those who pretend to give praise, and the narrowness of the space within which it is confined; and be quiet at last. For the whole earth is a point, and how small a corner of it is this dwelling of yours, and how few are there in it, and what kind of people are they who will praise you. This, then, remains: remember to retire into this little territory of your own, and above all do not distract or strain yourself, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal. But among the things readiest to your hand to turn to, let there be these two. One is that things do not touch the soul, for they are external and remain immovable; but our disturbances come only from the opinion within. The other is that all these things you see change immediately and will no longer be; and constantly bear in mind how many of these changes you have already witnessed. The universe is transformation: life is opinion.

4. If our intellectual part is common, the reason also, in respect of which we are rational beings, is common: if this is so, common also is the reason that commands us what to do and what not to do; if this is so, there is a common law also; if this is so, we are fellow citizens; if this is so, we are members of some political community; if this is so, the world is in a way a state. For of what other common political community will anyone say that the whole human race are members? And from there, from this common political community, come also our very intellectual faculty and reasoning faculty and our capacity for law; or where else do they come from? For as my earthly part is a portion given to me from certain earth, and what is watery from another element, and what is hot and fiery from some peculiar source (for nothing comes out of what is nothing, as nothing also returns to non-existence), so also the intellectual part comes from some source.

5. Death is such as birth is, a mystery of nature; a composition out of the same elements, and a decomposition into the same; and altogether not a thing of which any man should be ashamed, for it is not against the nature of a rational being, and not against the reason of our constitution.

6. It is natural that these things should be done by such persons; it is a matter of necessity; and if a man will not have it so, he will not allow the fig tree to have juice. But by all means bear this in mind, that within a very short time both you and he will be dead; and soon not even your names will be left behind.
7. Take away your opinion, and then the complaint, "I have been harmed," is taken away. Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
8. What does not make a man worse than he was also does not make his life worse, nor does it harm him either from without or from within.
9. The nature of what is universally useful has been compelled to do this.

10. Consider that everything that happens, happens justly, and if you observe carefully, you will find it to be so. I do not say only with respect to the continuity of the series of things, but with respect to what is just, and as if it were done by one who assigns to each thing its value. Observe, then, as you have begun; and whatever you do, do it together with this, being good, and in the sense in which a man is properly understood to be good. Keep to this in every action.
11. Do not have such an opinion of things as the man who does you wrong has, or such as he wishes you to have, but look at them as they are in truth.

12. A man should always have these two rules ready: one, to do only what the reason of the ruling and legislating part suggests for the use of men; the other, to change your opinion if there is anyone at hand who sets you right and moves you from any opinion. But this change of opinion must come only from a certain persuasion, as of what is just or for the common good, and the like, not because it appears pleasant or brings reputation.
13. Do you have reason? I have.—Why, then, do you not use it? For if this does its own work, what else do you want?
14. You have existed as a part. You will disappear into that which produced you; or rather, you will be received back into its generative principle by transformation.
15. Many grains of frankincense on the same altar: one falls before, another falls after; but it makes no difference.
16. Within ten days you will seem a god to those to whom you are now a beast and an ape, if you return to your principles and the worship of reason.
17. Do not act as if you were going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over you. While you live, while it is in your power, be good.

18. How much trouble he avoids who does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only to what he does himself, that it may be just and pure; or, as Agathon says, do not look round at the depraved morals of others, but run straight along the line without deviating from it.

19. He who has a vehement desire for fame after death does not consider that every one of those who remember him will himself also die very soon; then again also those who succeeded them, until the whole remembrance has been extinguished as it is passed on through men who foolishly admire and perish. But suppose that those who will remember are even immortal, and that the remembrance will be immortal, what then is this to you? And I do not say what is it to the dead, but what is it to the living? What is praise, except indeed so far as it has a certain utility? For you now unseasonably reject the gift of nature, clinging to something else....

20. Everything that is in any way beautiful is beautiful in itself, and ends in itself, not having praise as part of itself. A thing, then, is made neither worse nor better by being praised. I affirm this also of the things called beautiful by the common sort of men, for example, material things and works of art. What is really beautiful has no need of anything; no more than law, no more than truth, no more than kindness or modesty. Which of these things is beautiful because it is praised, or spoiled by being blamed? Is such a thing as an emerald made worse than it was if it is not praised? or gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a little knife, a flower, a shrub?

21. If souls continue to exist, how does the air contain them from eternity?—But how does the earth contain the bodies of those who have been buried from time so remote? For as here the change of these bodies after a certain continuance, whatever it may be, and their dissolution, make room for other dead bodies, so the souls that are removed into the air, after existing for some time, are transformed and diffused, and take on a fiery nature by being received into the generative intelligence of the universe, and in this way make room for the fresh souls that come to dwell there. And this is the answer a man might give on the hypothesis that souls continue to exist. But we must think not only of the number of bodies that are buried in this way, but also of the number of animals that are eaten daily by us and the other animals. For what a number is consumed, and so in a way buried in the bodies of those who feed on them! And nevertheless this earth receives them by reason of the changes of these bodies into blood, and their transformations into the aerial or the fiery element. What is the investigation into the truth in this matter? The division into that which is material and that which is the cause of form.
22. Do not be whirled about, but in every impulse have regard to justice, and on the occasion of every impression maintain the faculty of comprehension.

23. Everything harmonizes with me that is in harmony with you, O Universe. Nothing is too early or too late for me that is in due time for you. Everything is fruit to me that your seasons bring, O Nature: from you are all things, in you are all things, to you all things return. The poet says, Dear city of Cecrops; and will you not say, Dear city of Zeus?

24. Occupy yourself with few things, says the philosopher, if you would be calm.—But consider whether it would not be better to say, Do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of the being that is naturally social requires, and as it requires. For this brings not only the calm that comes from doing well, but also the calm that comes from doing few things. For since the greatest part of what we say and do is unnecessary, if a man takes this away, he will have more leisure and less uneasiness. Accordingly, on every occasion a man should ask himself, Is this one of the unnecessary things? Now a man should take away not only unnecessary acts, but also unnecessary thoughts, for then superfluous acts will not follow after.
25. Try how the life of the good man suits you, the life of him who is satisfied with his portion out of the whole, and satisfied with his own just acts and kind disposition.

26. Have you seen those things? Look also at these. Do not disturb yourself. Make yourself all simplicity. Does anyone do wrong? It is to himself that he does the wrong. Has anything happened to you? Well; out of the universe from the beginning everything that happens has been apportioned and spun out to you. In a word, your life is short. You must turn the present to profit with the aid of reason and justice. Be sober in your relaxation.

27. Either it is a well-arranged universe or a chaos huddled together, but still a universe. But can a certain order exist in you, and disorder in the whole? And this too when all things are so separated and diffused and in sympathy with one another.
28. A black character, a womanish character, a stubborn character, bestial, childish, animal, stupid, counterfeit, scurrilous, fraudulent, tyrannical.

29. If he is a stranger to the universe who does not know what is in it, no less is he a stranger who does not know what is going on in it. He is a runaway who flees from social reason; he is blind who shuts the eyes of the understanding; he is poor who has need of another, and does not have from himself all that is useful for life. He is an abscess on the universe who withdraws and separates himself from the reason of our common nature through being displeased with the things that happen, for the same nature produces this, and has produced you too: he is a piece torn off from the state who tears his own soul away from that of rational beings, which is one.

30. The one is a philosopher without a tunic, and the other without a book: here is another half naked: I have no bread, he says, and I abide by reason—and I do not get the means of living out of my learning, and I abide by my reason.

31. Love the art, poor as it may be, that you have learned, and be content with it; and pass through the rest of life like one who has entrusted to the gods with his whole soul all that he has, making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any man.

32. Consider, for example, the times of Vespasian. You will see all these things: people marrying, bringing up children, sick, dying, making war, feasting, trading, cultivating the ground, flattering, obstinately arrogant, suspecting, plotting, wishing for some to die, grumbling about the present, loving, heaping up treasure, desiring the consulship, kingly power. Well, then, that life of these people no longer exists at all. Again, move on to the times of Trajan. Again, all is the same. Their life too is gone. In the same way look also at the other epochs of time and of whole nations, and see how many, after great efforts, soon fell and were resolved into the elements. But chiefly you should think of those you have yourself known distracting themselves over idle things, neglecting to do what was in accordance with their proper constitution, and to hold firmly to this and be content with it. And here it is necessary to remember that the attention given to everything has its proper value and proportion. For then you will not be discontented, if you apply yourself to smaller matters no further than is fitting.

33. The words that were once familiar are now antiquated: so also the names of those who were famed of old are now in a way antiquated, Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Leonnatus, and a little after also Scipio and Cato, then Augustus, then also Hadrianus and Antoninus. For all things soon pass away and become a mere tale, and complete oblivion soon buries them. And I say this of those who have shone in a wondrous way. For the rest, as soon as they have breathed out their breath they are gone, and no man speaks of them. And, to conclude the matter, what is even an eternal remembrance? A mere nothing. What, then, is that on which we ought to employ our serious pains? This one thing: thoughts just, and acts social, and words that never lie, and a disposition that gladly accepts all that happens, as necessary, as usual, as flowing from a principle and source of the same kind.
34. Willingly give yourself up to Clotho, one of the fates, allowing her to spin your thread into whatever things she pleases.
35. Everything is only for a day, both what remembers and what is remembered.

36. Observe constantly that all things take place by change, and accustom yourself to consider that the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change the things that are and to make new things like them. For everything that exists is in a way the seed of what will be. But you are thinking only of seeds that are cast into the earth or into a womb: but this is a very commonplace notion.

37. You will soon die, and you are not yet simple, nor free from disturbances, nor without suspicion of being hurt by external things, nor kindly disposed toward all; nor do you yet place wisdom only in acting justly.
38. Examine men's ruling parts, even those of the wise, what kind of things they avoid, and what kind they pursue.

39. What is evil to you does not exist in the ruling part of another; nor yet in any turning and change of your bodily covering. Where is it, then? It is in that part of you in which the power of forming opinions about evils exists. Let this power, then, not form such opinions, and all is well. And if what is nearest to it, the poor body, is cut, burnt, filled with matter and rottenness, nevertheless let the part that forms opinions about these things be quiet; that is, let it judge that nothing is either bad or good which can happen equally to the bad man and the good. For what happens equally to him who lives against nature and to him who lives according to nature is neither according to nature nor against nature.

40. Constantly regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul; and observe how all things have reference to one perception, the perception of this one living being; and how all things act with one movement; and how all things are the cooperating causes of all things that exist; observe too the continuous spinning of the thread and the weave of the web.
41. You are a little soul carrying about a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.
42. It is no evil for things to undergo change, and no good for things to exist as a result of change.

43. Time is like a river made up of the events that happen, and a violent stream; for as soon as a thing has been seen, it is carried away, and another comes in its place, and this will be carried away too.

44. Everything that happens is as familiar and well known as the rose in spring and the fruit in summer; for such is disease, and death, and slander, and treachery, and whatever else delights fools or vexes them.

45. In the series of things, those that follow are always aptly fitted to those that have gone before: for this series is not like a mere enumeration of disjointed things, which has only a necessary sequence, but it is a rational connection: and as all existing things are arranged together harmoniously, so the things that come into existence show no mere succession, but a certain wonderful relationship.

46. Always remember the saying of Heraclitus, that the death of earth is to become water, and the death of water is to become air, and the death of air is to become fire, and the reverse. And think too of him who forgets where the way leads, and that men quarrel with that with which they are most constantly in communion, the reason that governs the universe; and the things they meet with daily seem to them strange: and consider that we ought not to act and speak as if we were asleep, for even in sleep we seem to act and speak; and that we ought not, like children who learn from their parents, simply to act and speak as we have been taught.

47. If any god told you that you will die tomorrow, or certainly on the day after tomorrow, you would not care much whether it was on the third day or tomorrow, unless you were mean-spirited in the highest degree; for how small the difference is! So think it no great thing to die after as many years as you can name rather than tomorrow.

48. Think continually how many physicians are dead after often contracting their eyebrows over the sick; and how many astrologers after predicting with great pretensions the deaths of others; and how many philosophers after endless discourses on death or immortality; how many heroes after killing thousands; and how many tyrants who have used their power over men's lives with terrible insolence, as if they were immortal; and how many cities are entirely dead, so to speak, Helice and Pompeii and Herculaneum, and others innumerable. Add to the reckoning all whom you have known, one after another. One man, after burying another, has been laid out dead, and another buries him; and all this in a short time. To conclude, always observe how ephemeral and worthless human things are, and what was yesterday a little mucus will tomorrow be a mummy or ashes. Pass, then, through this little space of time according to nature, and end your journey in content, as an olive falls off when it is ripe, blessing nature who produced it, and thanking the tree on which it grew.

49. Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it. Am I unhappy because this has happened to me? Not so; rather, I am happy, though this has happened to me, because I continue free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor fearing the future. For such a thing as this might have happened to every man; but not every man would have continued free from pain on such an occasion. Why, then, is that rather a misfortune than this a good fortune? And do you in all cases call that a man's misfortune which is not a deviation from man's nature? And does a thing seem to you to be a deviation from man's nature when it is not contrary to the will of man's nature? Well, you know the will of nature. Will, then, this that has happened prevent you from being just, magnanimous, temperate, prudent, secure against rash opinions and falsehood; will it prevent you from having modesty, freedom, and everything else by the presence of which man's nature obtains all that is its own? Remember too, on every occasion that leads you to resentment, to apply this principle: not that this is a misfortune, but that to bear it nobly is good fortune.

50. It is a commonplace, but still a useful help toward contempt of death, to pass in review those who have clung tenaciously to life. What more, then, have they gained than those who died early? Certainly they lie in their tombs somewhere at last, Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, or anyone else like them, who carried out many to be buried, and then were carried out themselves. Altogether the interval between birth and death is small; and consider with how much trouble, and in company with what sort of people, and in what a feeble body, this interval is laboriously passed. Do not then consider life a thing of any value. For look at the immensity of time behind you, and at the time before you, another boundless space. In this infinity, then, what is the difference between him who lives three days and him who lives three generations?

51. Always run by the short way; and the short way is the natural one: accordingly say and do everything in conformity with the soundest reason. For such a purpose frees a man from trouble, and warfare, and all artifice and ostentatious display.

chapters.title: Book 5
paragraphs: 1. In the morning, when you are reluctant to get up, keep this thought ready: I am getting up to do the work of a human being. Why, then, am I discontented, if I am going to do the things I exist for, the things I was brought into the world to do? Or was I made for this: to lie under the blankets and keep myself warm?—But this is more pleasant.—Do you exist, then, for pleasure, and not at all for action and effort? Do you not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders and the bees, all working together, each putting in order its own part of the universe? And are you unwilling to do the work of a human being? Do you not hurry to do what is in keeping with your nature?—But one must rest too.—One must. But nature has set limits to this as well, just as she has set limits to eating and drinking. Yet you go beyond those limits, beyond what is enough; while in your actions it is not so: there you stop short of what you could do. So you do not love yourself. If you did, you would love your nature and what she wills. Those who love their own crafts wear themselves out working at them, unwashed and unfed. But you value your own nature less than the wood-turner values his turning, or the dancer his dancing, or the money-lover his money, or the vain man his bit of glory. When such people are gripped by a passion for something, they would rather go without food and sleep than stop working at what they care about. Are the acts that serve the community worth less in your eyes, and less deserving of your effort?
2. How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troubling or out of place, and at once to be completely calm.

3. Judge every word and every act that is in keeping with nature to be worthy of you. Do not let yourself be turned aside by the criticism that may come from some people afterward, or by their talk. If something is good to do or to say, do not think it beneath you. Those people have their own ruling faculty and follow their own impulses. Pay no attention to that. Go straight on, following your own nature and the nature of the universe; and the two of them follow one and the same road.

4. I go on through the things that happen according to nature, until I fall and rest. Then I shall breathe out my last breath into the air from which I draw breath every day, and fall upon the earth from which my father gathered the seed, my mother the blood, and my nurse the milk; the earth that for so many years has given me food and drink; the earth that carries me when I walk on it and misuse it in so many ways.

5. You say: People cannot admire you for the sharpness of your wits.—Very well. But there are many other qualities of which you cannot say, "I was not made for that by nature." So show the qualities that are entirely in your power: sincerity, seriousness, endurance of hard work, turning away from pleasure, contentment with your lot and with little, kindness, frankness, no love of excess, freedom from triviality, greatness of spirit. Do you not see how many qualities you could show right now, where you have no excuse of lacking the natural gift or the aptitude? And yet you still choose to stay below the mark. Or is it because nature made you badly that you are forced to grumble, to be mean, to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please people, to show off, and to be so restless in your mind? No, by the gods! You could have been rid of all these things long ago. Only, if in truth you can be charged with being somewhat slow and dull to understand, then you must work at that too, neither neglecting it nor taking pleasure in your dullness.

6. One person, when he has done someone a kindness, is quick to put it down to that person's account as a favor owed. Another is not quick to do this, but privately he still thinks of the other as in his debt, and he knows what he has done. A third, in a sense, does not even know what he has done. He is like a vine that has produced grapes and asks for nothing more once it has borne its proper fruit. A horse that has run its race, a dog that has hunted down its prey, a bee that has made its honey: so a person who has done a good deed does not call others to come and see, but goes on to the next, as a vine goes on to bear grapes again in their season.—Must a person, then, be one of those who act this way almost without noticing it?—Yes.—But surely one must notice what one is doing. For, it may be said, it is the mark of a being made for community to be aware that he is acting for the community, and indeed to want his partner in the community to be aware of it too.—What you say is true. But you have misunderstood what is being said now, and because of that you will become one of those I spoke of first; for they too are led astray by something that looks like reason. But if you choose to understand what is being said, do not fear that because of it you will neglect any act that serves the community.
7. A prayer of the Athenians: "Rain, rain, dear Zeus, on the plowed fields of the Athenians and on the plains." In truth, we ought either not to pray at all, or to pray in this simple and noble way.

8. When people say that Aesculapius prescribed horse-riding for this man, or cold baths, or going barefoot, we understand what they mean. In the same way we should understand it when people say that the nature of the universe prescribed for this man disease, or maiming, or loss, or anything else of the kind. In the first case "prescribed" means roughly this: he ordered it for this man as something suited to bring about his health. In the second case it means that what happens to each person has been arranged for him in a way that fits his destiny. For this is what we mean when we say that things "fit" us, just as builders say that the squared stones in walls or in pyramids "fit," when they set them together in a certain arrangement. For in the whole there is only one fitting together, one harmony. And just as the universe is made up out of all bodies to be the kind of body it is, so necessity, or destiny, is made up out of all existing causes to be the kind of cause it is. Even people who know nothing of all this understand what I mean, for they say: "Destiny brought this on him."—So this was brought on him, and this was prescribed for him. Let us accept these things, then, as we accept what Aesculapius prescribes. Many of his prescriptions too are unpleasant, of course, but we welcome them in the hope of health. Let the completion and fulfillment of what the nature of the universe judges good be, in your judgment, the same kind of thing as your own health. So welcome everything that happens, even if it seems unpleasant, because it leads to this: to the health of the universe, and to the well-being and happiness of Zeus, that is, of the universe. For he would not have brought on anyone what he has brought, if it were not useful for the whole. Nor does the nature of anything, whatever it may be, bring about anything that does not suit what it governs. So there are two reasons why it is right to be content with what happens to you. The first is that it happened to you, was prescribed for you, and was in some way related to you, spun into your destiny from the beginning out of the most ancient causes. The second is that even what comes to each person individually contributes to the well-being and completion of the power that governs the universe, and indeed to its very continuance. For the whole is maimed if you cut off anything at all from the connection and continuity of its parts, or of its causes. And you do cut something off, as far as you are able, whenever you are discontented, and in a way try to get rid of something.

9. Do not be disgusted, or give up, or lose heart, if you do not manage to do everything according to right principles. When you have failed, go back again, and be content if most of what you do is in keeping with human nature; and love the thing you are going back to. Do not go back to philosophy as though she were a master, but as people with sore eyes go back to their bit of sponge and egg, or as someone else turns to a plaster or a dousing with water. In this way you will not fail to obey reason, and you will find rest in it. And remember that philosophy wants only what your nature wants; but you want something else, something that is not in keeping with nature.—Yes, but what could be more pleasant than this, the thing I am doing?—But is this not exactly how pleasure deceives us? Consider whether greatness of spirit, freedom, simplicity, good temper and reverence for the gods are not more pleasant. And what is more pleasant than wisdom itself, when you think how secure and how smooth-running is everything that depends on the power of understanding and knowing?

10. Things are wrapped in such obscurity that quite a few philosophers, and not ordinary ones, have thought them entirely beyond understanding. Even the Stoics themselves find them hard to understand. And all our assent is liable to change; for where is the person who never changes? Then turn your thoughts to the things themselves, and see how short-lived and worthless they are, and how they can be owned by a filthy wretch, a prostitute or a robber. Next, turn to the characters of the people you live with: even the most agreeable of them is hard to put up with, not to mention that a person can hardly put up with himself. In such darkness and dirt, and in so constant a flow of substance and of time, of movement and of things moved, I cannot imagine what there is that deserves to be highly valued, or even seriously pursued. On the contrary, a person should comfort himself and wait for his natural breaking up, and not be irritated at the delay, but find rest in these two principles alone. The first: nothing will happen to me that is not in keeping with the nature of the universe. The second: it is in my power never to act against my god and the divine spirit within me; for no one can force me to do that.

11. What am I using my soul for now? On every occasion I must ask myself this, and examine myself: What is there now in this part of me that people call the ruling faculty? And whose soul do I have now? A child's, a young man's, a weak woman's, a tyrant's, a farm animal's, or a wild beast's?

12. Even from this we can learn what sort of things the many take to be good. If someone has first thought of certain things as truly good, such as practical wisdom, self-control, justice and courage, then once he has that idea in his mind he could not bear to hear anything said that clashed with what is truly good. But if someone has first thought of the things the many take to be good, he will listen to the line of the comic poet, and gladly accept it as right on target. So even the many sense the difference. Otherwise the joke would not offend us and be rejected when applied to the first kind of good, while we accept it as apt and witty when it is said of wealth, and of the things that bring luxury and fame. Go on, then, and ask whether we should value and think good those things which, once they come to mind, invite the comic poet's line: that their owner is so rich he has no room left to relieve himself.

13. I am made of form and matter—what shapes me and what I am made of. Neither of them will vanish into nothing, just as neither came into being out of nothing. So every part of me will be changed into some part of the universe, and that in turn will change into another part of the universe, and so on forever. It was through such a change that I too came to be, and my parents before me, and so on forever in the other direction. For nothing prevents us from saying this, even if the universe is governed in fixed cycles.

14. Reason, and the art of reasoning, are powers sufficient for themselves and for their own work. So they start from a first principle of their own and make their way to the goal set before them. That is why acts of this kind are called Catorthoseis, or right acts: the word means that they go by the right road.

15. None of these things should be called a person's own that do not belong to a person as a human being. They are not required of a human being; human nature does not promise them; and they are not the means by which human nature reaches its goal. So the goal of a human being does not lie in these things, nor does what helps him reach that goal—and what helps him reach it is the good. Besides, if any of these things did belong to a human being, it would not be right for him to despise them and set himself against them. Nor would someone deserve praise for showing that he does not need them; nor would someone who went without any of them be good—if these things were really good. But as it is, the more of these things, or of others like them, a person goes without, or the more patiently he bears being deprived of any of them, the better a person he is, in exactly that degree.

16. As your habitual thoughts are, so your mind will be; for the soul is dyed by its thoughts. So dye it with a steady stream of thoughts like these. For example: wherever a person can live, he can also live well. But he must live in a palace.—Very well, then he can also live well in a palace. And again: whatever each thing was made for, that is what it was made for, and that is what it moves toward. Its goal lies in what it moves toward; and where its goal is, there too is its benefit and its good. Now the good of a rational being is community; for it has been shown already that we are made for community. Is it not plain that the lower exists for the sake of the higher? And living things are higher than lifeless things, and among living things the higher are those that have reason.
17. To pursue the impossible is madness; and it is impossible that bad people should not do things of this kind.

18. Nothing happens to anyone that he is not made by nature to bear.
